timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello, my name is Bradley Martin and I am a PhD student work of my supervisor,
Jarvis Frost, in the Experimental Solidestate Group at Imperial College London,
where I am researching how to develop better theories for better mobilities.
Why is mobility important? Well, mobility affects whether a material will perform well as say a solar panel,
an LED or a battery. It is a very important property of any semiconductor material.
So why better theories? Well, because materials are complicated and
mobility is determined by complex quantum processes,
mobility is commonly calculated using semi-classical models such as the drood model,
but we want to include more material properties and treat mobility quantumly.
So where do we begin? A good start and point was provided by Herbert Frouelik in the 1950s,
who developed a Hamiltonian that describes a single conduction band electron
interacting with the polarization field in a material.
The strength of the interaction is characterized by the dimensionless alpha parameter,
which can be determined from material properties.
This scenario can be pictures as an electron repellent negative ions than attracts
impositive ions, the self-induced potential arises, which acts back on the electron and
modifies its properties. This can also be viewed as an electron dress with a virtual cloud
of phonons that move with the electron through the material, collectively known as a polaron.
Frouelik's model has no known exact solution.
Therefore, we see an approximate solution, so we copy Richard Feynman and use path integrals.
These focus on all the possible trajectories that the polaron can take.
The result is that the infinite number of phonons can instead be replaced with an effective
potential. This potential looks like an attractive cool-on potential between the electron
and itself at an earlier time.
The caveat is that we are now working in an imaginary time, which replaces troublesome
oscillations of exponential decays, as what quantum physics falls statistical physics.
From this, we can get a variational principle that gives the n upper bounds to the free
energy of the polaron by swapping out the effective cool-on potential for an effective harmonic
potential.
Now back to mobility. We start by finding the best harmonic approximation to the polaron,
which looks like the electron coupled by spring to a fictitious particle standing in
for every phonon. The mobility is given by the zero-frequency limit of the real conductivity
of the electron, with a quantum part of the responses entirely contained in a memory
function that we calculate with the harmonic model.
The result are non-drewed like oscillations that alter the polaront mobility.
I have extended Feynman's model to include multiple phonon modes, which replaces the
single spring approximation by one where the electron is coupled by springs to many fictitious
particles with different vibrational frequencies and masses. This allows us to more accurately
model the polaron quantum response to give better predictions for the conductivity spectra
of materials.
Thank you for watching and please check out our code over on GitHub.

youtube_description:
An introduction talk to my research on using path integrals to extend the Fröhlich polaron model. I made the video as a fun project to succinctly describe my PhD project. The aim is to make the theory more inclusive of material properties such as multiple phonon modes, anisotropy and anharmonicity. 

Check out my GitHub here: https://github.com/Neutrino155
The open source code associated with this video can be found at the following repository:  https://github.com/jarvist/PolaronMobility.jl

I took inspiration from the video style used by Minute Physics:
https://www.youtube.com/user/minutephysics

whose videos I love to watch! Although, I did not use stop-motion, I instead used an iPad and screen recorded myself drawing everything on the Procreate app.
youtube_title: How Mobile is an Electron? Using Path Integrals to Describe Polaron Formation and Mobility
